newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Palladium trade says nobody defaulted.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Palladium trade says nobody defaulted.

text.p: Market makers in palladium vowed on Thursday to try to promote order in their market but said that the end of an acute shortage of the rare white metal, that has led to spiral in prices, depended on Russia resuming delayed exports.
"The members confirmed that there were no defaults in the market," said Trevor Pitts, chairman of the London Platinum and Palladium Market Association, after urgent talks on the situation.

Rumours of the possibility of a default on delivery had been the latest scare in a market bedevilled by delay in supply from Russia, the biggest exporter, and a build-up of big speculative fund holdings of metal.
Pitts chaired talks of 10 full members of the market plus three Zurich-based clearing members who joined in on the telephone.

"We called the meeting in response to concerns about the tightness in the market...The members agreed to try to offer clients an orderly market in platinum and palladium. The key issue really depends on when the Russians begin exporting again," Pitts said.
Prices on palladium - used in electronics, chemicals, dentistry and auto catalystic coverters -- were particularly wild on Thursday.
"It's a hairy situation...volatility is huge today," said analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Global Mining Group.

Spot palladium prices lurched back and forth, surging to $235.00 per ounce, at the highest since 1980, then slid later. New York futures late on Thursday were just below $220. Prices have risen 100 percent since the start of the year.
Pitts said that in a measure to help the market forward rates would be done but only on a "quote suggestion" basis, meaning there was no absolute contractual commitment, for the time being.
Dealers had stopped quoting forward rates for palladium after the cost of borrowing it surged to around 300 percent for one-month metal.

Players borrow metal, rather than buy, when they think high prices won't last - a prospect that could arise when the Russians eventually start exporting again, or if speculative funds liquidate positions.

"The problem was nobody had the stuff to lend and when some people detected this they insisted on delivery of the physical metal, not cash," a senior dealer said. If a firm could not meet its obligation, as a last resort it could be expelled from the market for a period, he added.

The informal market is self-regulated by the London Platinum and Palladium Market Association since the two metals are not traded on an exchange, British official regulatory officials said. The Bank of England has no oversight over them, a spokeswoman said.
Pitts said market-makers were under obligation to quote spot rates but not forward ones for the platinum group metals, although they traditionally did so.
Lack of Russian supplies has been compounded by speculative buying by investment funds. The U.S. Tiger Management Fund is said to be holding 1.5 million ounces of palladium.
Funds are reluctant to open the floodgates since each time they dribble out small parcels of the metal, prices start to crumble, one dealer said.
"The funds have to play this very delicately if they are to have a profitable position," he said.

Russia supplies 60 percent of world palladium and about 20 percent of platinum, but fiscal and administrative problems and a possible change of marketing strategy led to a suspension of exports last December.
Palladium's sister metal platinum surged to fix at $442 per ounce on Thursday afternoon, the strongest since July 19, 1995.

Users of both the metals had expected Russian shipments to resume by now and had been borrowing metal to cover their needs. Russian officials told Japanese traders on Wednesday that Russian platinum and palladium exports would resume on June 20, but they also said the export licences had still not yet been granted by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations.
